reference.source: Resnick Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders
clinicalPearls: Ribbing disease is a rare sclerosing dysplasia characterised by endosteal and periosteal new bone formation confined to the diaphyses of the long bones, most often the tibia and femur.
It typically presents after puberty in adults, distinguishing it from the childhood-onset Camurati-Engelmann disease it otherwise resembles radiologically.
Involvement is often asymmetrical and may be limited to one or a few bones, unlike the symmetrical pattern of Camurati-Engelmann disease.
The dominant symptom is deep, activity-related bone pain in the affected limb, and many cases are discovered when investigating unexplained leg pain.
There is no associated myopathy, cranial involvement or systemic features, which helps separate it from diaphyseal dysplasia with neuromuscular signs.
Bone scintigraphy shows increased uptake at active sites and helps map disease and exclude alternative causes of sclerosis.
It is frequently a diagnosis of exclusion after osteoid osteoma, chronic osteomyelitis, and sclerosing malignancy have been ruled out.
Management is largely symptomatic; the pain can be difficult to control and the natural history is variable.
reference.pathophysiology: Ribbing disease is a disorder of bone modelling in which excessive endosteal and periosteal apposition thickens the diaphyseal cortex and narrows the medullary canal. The molecular basis is incompletely understood; some pedigrees suggest autosomal recessive inheritance, and it is regarded by many authorities as part of a spectrum with Camurati-Engelmann disease, which is linked to activating mutations in the TGF-beta 1 gene that increase osteoblastic bone formation. Unlike the generalised, symmetrical, childhood-onset TGF-beta 1 disorder, Ribbing disease is later in onset, focal and asymmetrical, and spares the skull and the neuromuscular system, implying a distinct or attenuated mechanism of dysregulated diaphyseal bone turnover.
additionalInvestigations: plain radiography of the long bones for diaphyseal cortical thickening
bone scintigraphy to localise active lesions
MRI to assess marrow and exclude a nidus or tumour
CT to characterise cortical sclerosis and exclude an osteoid osteoma nidus
inflammatory markers and cultures to exclude infection
family history assessment and, where indicated, TGFB1 gene testing
redFlags: night pain unresponsive to rest suggesting osteoid osteoma or malignancy
systemic features such as fever or weight loss pointing to infection or tumour
a soft-tissue mass or cortical destruction on imaging
reference.prognosis: Ribbing disease is benign and does not undergo malignant transformation, but chronic bone pain may be persistent and refractory, and the clinical course fluctuates over years.
pitfalls: Mistaking focal diaphyseal sclerosis for osteosarcoma or metastasis and proceeding to aggressive intervention.
Overlooking a small osteoid osteoma nidus within thickened cortex.
Assuming symmetry and thereby confusing it with Camurati-Engelmann disease.
Attributing the pain to soft-tissue causes and delaying dedicated bone imaging.
Performing unnecessary biopsy when the radiological and clinical picture is characteristic.
references: Resnick Diagnosis of Bone and Joint Disorders, current edition
Taybi and Lachman Radiology of Syndromes, Metabolic Disorders and Skeletal Dysplasias
management: Analgesia with simple analgesics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for the chronic activity-related diaphyseal bone pain, as no disease-modifying treatment exists
Bisphosphonates trialled for refractory pain, recognising that response is inconsistent
Corticosteroids considered by analogy with the related Camurati-Engelmann disease, though evidence in Ribbing disease is limited
Exclude infection, osteoid osteoma and malignancy with imaging, cultures and biopsy before committing to long-term management
Activity modification and physiotherapy to reduce mechanical pain
Surgical intramedullary reaming or cortical decompression in selected cases of intractable pain
Reassurance about the benign, non-malignant nature with long-term follow-up given the fluctuating course
